title: Build a LoRa mesh node from parts
summary: A small radio that sends text messages for kilometres with no phone network or internet, passing them on through other nodes. Use a ready LoRa board, or wire a bare SX1262 radio module to an ESP32, nRF52840 or Raspberry Pi Pico. Flash the free Meshtastic firmware, set it up, and build a quarter-wave ground-plane antenna from wire and an old coax socket.

materials.item: Microcontroller board: nRF52840 "Pro Micro" clone (lowest draw), ESP32 DevKit or Raspberry Pi Pico. Skip this and the radio if you use a ready LoRa board (Heltec V3, LilyGO T-Beam or T3S3, RAK WisBlock)

LoRa radio for your band (433, 868 or 915 MHz): SX1262 module (Ebyte E22-900M22S, 3.3 V supply, never above 3.7 V; E22-900M30S, 1 W, 2.5–5.5 V; Heltec HT-RA62; Waveshare Pico-LoRa-SX1262). SX1276 (RFM95W): only the nRF52 Pro Micro target, untested; not recommended for new builds
50 Ω antenna for your band with a matching plug (SMA and RP-SMA do not fit each other), or the parts below to build one
For the ground plane: a panel socket (N, SO-239, BNC or SMA) and stiff copper or brass wire, about 1.3–2 mm across (16–12 AWG), e.g. solid house wire or brazing rod
materials.qty: 1 socket, 0.5 m wire (1 m for 433 MHz)

materials.item: 50 Ω coax with an adapter to the node: RG-58 for short runs, LMR-400 or better for anything over a few metres
Battery: an 18650 Li-ion cell (flat-top unprotected for a T-Beam, protected for a LilyGO T3), or a LiFePO4 cell with its own charger
Single-cell Li-ion charge board with protection, for DIY builds with no charger
Thin hookup wire, 0.2–0.35 mm² (24–22 AWG), for the radio wiring
Capacitors at the module supply: a small ceramic right at VCC, plus an electrolytic for a 1 W module
Plastic box (not metal) with a cable gland, and a membrane vent if it lives outdoors
USB data cable (charge-only cables carry no data)
GPS module, small OLED display or INA219 current sensor

steps.text: Find your country on the LoRa bands card and note its band and Meshtastic region (Canada and the US: 902–928 MHz, region US). Check that the band printed on the board or module (433, 868 or 915) matches before you buy, strip or wire anything.

While you still have internet, put everything from "Flashing with no internet" in the notes on a USB stick: the Stable (not Alpha) firmware zip for your chip, esptool and the Meshtastic command-line tool as downloaded wheels, the Android app's .apk, the USB serial drivers your computer needs, the factory-erase .uf2 for your chip and, for nRF52 boards, the bootloader packages.

DIY only: wire the radio to the board with short wires, following the wiring table in the notes: NSS, SCK, MOSI, MISO, NRST, BUSY and DIO1, plus RXEN and TXEN on modules with an outside RF switch. With an E22 on a Pro Micro, join the module's DIO2 to its own TXEN.
steps.warn: Logic is 3.3 V: 5 V on a radio or board pin can destroy it. Solder with ventilation and wash your hands; old solder contains lead.

steps.text: DIY only: wire the radio's supply from a clean source with a shared ground, but leave everything unplugged and switched off until the antenna is fitted (next step). A 22 dBm module can share the board's 3.3 V pin if that pin is rated for it; feed a 1 W E22-900M30S (2.5–5.5 V, 650 mA when sending) from the battery or its own regulator, good for at least 850 mA (650 mA plus Ebyte's 30 % margin). Put a ceramic capacitor right at the module's VCC and GND, and add an electrolytic for the 1 W module.
steps.warn: Reversed polarity or too high a supply can kill an E22. The 1 W E22-900M30S takes 5.5 V at most; the E22-900M22S and bare SX1262 or SX1276 modules about 3.7 V: never 5 V or a full 4.2 V Li-ion cell, only regulated 3.3 V. Check polarity and voltage with a meter first.

steps.text: Fit an antenna before the radio ever gets power, and leave it on. Setting the region in step 7 is what lets the node start sending. If you have no bought antenna, do step 8 now and fit the finished ground plane here, before you flash or configure anything.
steps.warn: Transmitting with no antenna, or a badly matched one, reflects power back and can damage the radio.

steps.text: Flash Meshtastic. ESP32: run device-install with the firmware file. nRF52: double-press reset and copy the .uf2 file onto the drive that appears. Pico: hold BOOTSEL while plugging in and copy the .uf2. DIY builds use the NRF52 Pro-micro DIY, Hydra (ESP32 with E22) or Raspberry Pi Pico firmware.
steps.warn: The wrong bootloader can brick an nRF52 board. Check the board name and file name twice.

steps.text: Connect with the phone app over Bluetooth, or the command-line tool over USB. Set the region first, then the names, role CLIENT, and the preset and channels your area uses. Leave transmit power at 0 unless a 1 W module or a high-gain antenna takes you over your country's limit.

Build the ground-plane antenna (do this before step 5 if it is your only antenna): cut the radiator and four radials a few millimetres long (table in the notes). Solder the radiator to the socket's centre pin and one radial to each corner of its flange, then bend the radials down about 45°.
steps.warn: Cut wire ends are sharp. File them round or cap them, especially on an antenna at head height.

steps.text: Tune it: with an antenna analyser or SWR meter that really measures up to your frequency (many meters stop far below 868/915 MHz, and the original NanoVNA stops at 900 MHz), trim the radiator 1 mm at a time for the lowest reading at your frequency. Without one, compare the SNR another fixed node reports for each antenna, and keep the better one.
steps.warn: Turn Transmit Enabled off in the LoRa settings before each antenna swap, and back on after, so the node never sends into an open socket.

steps.text: Fit the battery: test the cell first, check the plug's polarity with a meter, then plug it into the board's battery socket. DIY boards need a protected charge board between cell and node. LiFePO4 gets its own LiFePO4 charger. Charging a frozen cell plates metallic lithium on the anode, and a node in an outdoor box on a solar panel or USB charger will do exactly that on a cold, sunny day unless its charger stops on cell temperature.
steps.warn: Damaged, swollen, reversed or overcharged lithium cells can burn. Never leave a new build charging unattended, never put LiFePO4 on a 4.2 V Li-ion charger, and never charge any lithium cell below 0 °C (32 °F) or above 45 °C (113 °F).

steps.text: Box it: plastic box, antenna outside and pointing straight up, cables through a gland with a drip loop below. Add a membrane vent to a box that lives outdoors.

Range test with a second node: turn on the Range Test module on both, set the fixed node to send every 30 s (LongFast), carry this one with a phone for position, and note where the numbered messages stop. Turn the sender off afterwards; it also stops itself after 8 hours (Meshtastic range test).
steps.warn: Don't climb onto roofs or masts alone to place a test node. A 2 m fall can kill: use a ladder with a second person.

notes:
Frequency rules by country are on the [LoRa bands card](#ref/reference_lora_bands); board resets, drivers and boot buttons on [Microcontrollers](#ref/reference_microcontrollers). To link many nodes across a town, see [LoRa mesh network for a whole town](#guides/build_lora_town_mesh).

## Pick a path

Meshtastic says nRF52 boards use less power than ESP32 boards and suit solar and handhelds; ESP32 boards cost less and add Wi-Fi. It strongly recommends the newer SX126x radios over SX127x (Meshtastic devices). The SX1262 chip covers 150–960 MHz at up to +22 dBm (Semtech SX1262), but each module is built for one band.

| Board | Inside | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Heltec WiFi LoRa 32 V3 | ESP32-S3, SX1262 | Li-ion socket with charging; may not charge over a USB-C to USB-C cable (Meshtastic Heltec). [Pinout](#ref/pinouts/heltec_wifi_lora32_v3) |
| LilyGO T-Beam | ESP32-S3 (Supreme, S3-Core, 1W), SX1262, GPS | All models except the S3-Core have an 18650 holder built to the original spec, so it takes only unprotected flat-top cells; protected and button-top cells are usually too long (Meshtastic T-Beam) |
| LilyGO T3 V1.6.1 | ESP32, SX127x | Meshtastic does not recommend it for new purchases or unattended nodes and is phasing out firmware support, and early boards had a wrong part in the LiPo charging circuit that lets the battery be overcharged (boards bought after 2021 should not, except one marked T3_v1.6 20180606). If you still use one: protected cell, and never leave it charging unattended. Meshtastic suggests the T3S3 instead (Meshtastic T-LoRa). [Pinout](#ref/pinouts/lilygo_lora32_t3_v161) |
| RAK WisBlock (RAK19007 base, RAK4631 core) | nRF52840, SX1262 | 3.7 V Li-ion on a JST PHR-2 plug, 4.3 V max; 5 V solar input, 5.5 V max; 350 mA charging (RAK19007). Buy the RAK4631 (H) for 868/915 MHz (the (L) is 433/470 MHz) and not the RAK4631-R, which needs a different bootloader (RAK4631, Meshtastic UF2) |
| DIY: nRF52840 Pro Micro + SX1262 module | Firmware NRF52 Pro-micro DIY | Wiring below (Meshtastic Pro Micro) |
| DIY: ESP32 DevKit + Ebyte E22 | Firmware Hydra | Wiring below (Meshtastic Hydra). [DevKit pinout](#ref/pinouts/esp32_devkitc_v4) |
| DIY: Pico + Waveshare Pico-LoRa-SX1262 | Firmware Raspberry Pi Pico | Plugs together. No Bluetooth; the Pico W has Wi-Fi only; keep the antenna away from the USB port (Meshtastic Pico). [Pinout](#ref/pinouts/raspberry_pi_pico) |

## Wiring

| Signal | E22 pin | Pro Micro | ESP32 DevKit (Hydra) |
|---|---|---|---|
| NSS (chip select) | 19 | P1.13 | GPIO18 |
| SCK | 18 | P1.11 | GPIO5 |
| MOSI | 17 | P1.15 | GPIO27 |
| MISO | 16 | P0.02 | GPIO19 |
| NRST (reset) | 15 | P0.09 | GPIO23 |
| BUSY | 14 | P0.29 | GPIO32 |
| DIO1 | 13 | P0.10 | GPIO33 |
| RXEN | 6 | P0.17 | GPIO14 |
| TXEN | 7 | To the module's own DIO2 (pin 8) | GPIO13 |
| VCC | E22-900M30S: 9 and 10. E22-900M22S: 9 only, because its pin 10 is GND | See power | See power |
| GND | 1–5, 11, 12, 20, 22 (E22-900M22S: also 10) | Gnd | GND |

Pins from the Meshtastic firmware's variant files (Meshtastic Pro Micro, Meshtastic Hydra) and Ebyte's pin table (Ebyte E22). On the E22, DIO2 may drive TXEN but must not go to a microcontroller pin; DIO3 runs the module's crystal (Ebyte E22). Modules with a built-in RF switch, such as the Heltec HT-RA62, need no RXEN or TXEN wires (Meshtastic Pro Micro). The pin numbers in the table are for the 22-pad Ebyte E22 only; wire other modules by signal name from their own datasheet. On an E22 the antenna goes to its u.FL (IPEX) socket or to stamp-hole pin 21 (50 Ω): use one of the two (Ebyte E22). An RFM95W on the Pro Micro uses the BUSY wire as DIO0 (Meshtastic Pro Micro). Pico HAT: NSS GP3, SCK GP10, MOSI GP11, MISO GP12, RESET GP15, BUSY GP2, DIO1 GP20 (Waveshare Pico-LoRa-SX1262).

## Power and 3.3 V

- **Logic is 3.3 V.** ESP32 pins take 3.6 V at most ([Microcontrollers](#ref/reference_microcontrollers)). Ebyte says to add level conversion for 5 V logic (Ebyte E22).
- **Bare radios** run on about 3.3 V: RFM95W 2.4–3.7 V (HopeRF RFM95W), SX1262 in the RAK4631 2.0–3.7 V (RAK4631), E22-900M22S 1.8–3.7 V (Ebyte E22 M22S). Do not feed any of them 5 V or a full 4.2 V cell.
- **E22-900M30S (1 W)** is the exception: supply 2.5–5.5 V, 5 V recommended, over 5.5 V permanent damage; 650 mA when transmitting; reversed supply can destroy it. Ebyte asks for a ceramic filter capacitor close to VCC and GND, a supply with 30 % spare, and a reliable ground (Ebyte E22). The Heltec V3's 3V3 pin gives 500 mA at most ([pinout](#ref/pinouts/heltec_wifi_lora32_v3)), so feed a 1 W module from the battery or its own regulator, grounds joined.
- **Its amplifier adds about 8 dB:** 22 dBm from the SX1262 gives about 30 dBm out (Meshtastic Hydra). That matches the 30 dBm ceiling Meshtastic applies to the US region, which is a firmware ceiling and not your legal limit (the legal limit also counts antenna gain: see the [LoRa bands](#ref/reference_lora_bands) card). Ebyte lists the output as 29.5–31 dBm. Meshtastic's transmit power setting is the SX1262's own output, capped at 22 dBm, and the amplifier adds its 8 dB after it, so in the US region (limit 30 dBm) and in EU_868 (limit 27 dBm) a setting of 0 gives about 30 dBm out. In Europe's 869.4–869.65 MHz band the cap is 27 dBm (500 mW) ERP, so set the transmit power about 8 dB below the limit you want, for example 19 dBm for about 27 dBm out, and check the real output with a power meter if you can (Meshtastic LoRa, Meshtastic Hydra, Ebyte E22).

## Flashing with no internet

The web flasher needs Chrome or Edge and the internet (Meshtastic web flasher). Download now and keep on a stick:

- The firmware release file for your chip (for a Heltec V3, firmware-esp32s3) from Meshtastic's Downloads page (Meshtastic ESP32 CLI).
- esptool and the command-line tool: Meshtastic's `pip3 install --upgrade ...` commands download from the internet and install on this computer only, so they put nothing on the stick. While online, on a computer with the same operating system and Python version as the one you will flash from, run `pip3 download esptool "meshtastic[cli]" -d wheels` (add `pytap2` on Linux and Windows) and copy the `wheels` folder to the stick. Offline, install with `pip3 install --no-index --find-links wheels esptool "meshtastic[cli]"`. Python 3 must already be installed there (Meshtastic ESP32 CLI, Meshtastic CLI, pip download).
- The Android app: save the .apk from the app's F-Droid page; installing through the F-Droid store app needs the internet (Meshtastic downloads).
- nRF52 bootloader packages (Meshtastic bootloader).

Then flash:

- **ESP32:** in the unzipped folder run `./device-install.sh -f firmware-BOARD-VERSION.bin` (Windows: `device-install.bat`); updates use `device-update.sh` with the `-update.bin` file (Meshtastic ESP32 CLI).
- **nRF52:** double-press reset; a drive with CURRENT.UF2, INDEX.HTM and INFO_UF2.TXT appears; copy the firmware .uf2 onto it. A board stuck in a crash loop after an upgrade needs a factory erase (Meshtastic UF2). Meshtastic's bootloader page has packages for DIY nRF52 boards (Meshtastic bootloader).
- **Pico:** hold BOOTSEL while plugging in, then copy the .uf2 (Meshtastic UF2, which covers RP2040 and RP2350).

## First settings

1. **Region.** Meshtastic will not transmit until it is set (Meshtastic LoRa). Canada and the US: US.
2. **Preset.** Ask the local group which preset it uses and set it yourself. LongFast (LONG_FAST) is the default when the region is set from the phone app or the command line, but a US node whose region is set from its own screen starts on LONG_TURBO, which cannot hear LONG_FAST nodes, and many busy towns have moved to faster presets. Nodes only hear each other when region, preset and channel match (Meshtastic joining, Meshtastic LoRa).
3. **Role.** CLIENT (the default, and Meshtastic's advice when in doubt). CLIENT_MUTE for extra radios in the same house or place: make one of them CLIENT and the rest CLIENT_MUTE. ROUTER only for a fixed node on a carefully chosen high site: Meshtastic calls it suitable only for stationary devices in extremely strategic locations, and a badly placed router costs the whole mesh range (Meshtastic role blog).
4. **Names.** Long and short names. Licensed hams: turn on licensed mode, put your call sign in the long name and empty the channel key so nothing is encrypted; the command-line option --set-ham does all three (Meshtastic user).
5. **Channels.** Keep the default primary; add private groups as secondary channels. Renaming the primary changes the frequency and can cut you off (Meshtastic joining).
6. **Transmit power** 0 means the region's default maximum, but that is the firmware's ceiling, not your law (Meshtastic LoRa).

## Quarter-wave ground-plane antenna

Wavelength λ (mm) = 299,792 ÷ frequency (MHz). Radiator = 0.25 λ × 0.95; radials = 0.28 λ × 0.95, about 12 % longer. Use four radials (three at least, up to six), bent down about 45°, which raises the feed impedance from about 36 Ω to about 50 Ω (m0ukd); an exact 50 Ω match is at 42° (Electronics Notes). Cut a little long and trim (m0ukd).

| Band | Cut for | Radiator | Each radial |
|---|---|---|---|
| US, Canada (902–928) | 915 MHz | 78 mm (3.06 in) | 87 mm (3.43 in) |
| Europe (869.4–869.65) | 869.5 MHz | 82 mm (3.22 in) | 92 mm (3.61 in) |
| 433 MHz | 433.9 MHz | 164 mm (6.46 in) | 184 mm (7.24 in) |

Lengths calculated for this guide (c = 299,792 km/s, so λ in mm = 299,792 ÷ f in MHz). Meshtastic has no licence-free 433 MHz region for the Americas: in Canada and the US 433 MHz is the 70 cm amateur band, usable only with an amateur licence, in licensed mode with your call sign and no encryption (Meshtastic LoRa). Solder the radiator to the centre pin of a panel socket (N, SO-239, BNC or SMA) and the radials to its flange. Mount it vertical.

**Coax eats signal at 900 MHz.** RG-58 loses 13.7 dB per 100 ft (Belden 8240), LMR-400 3.9 dB (Times LMR-400). Over 10 m (33 ft) RG-58 keeps 36 % of your power, LMR-400 74 %. Putting the node outside often beats a long cable (Meshtastic antennas). TV coax is 75 Ω: short runs work, with a 1.5:1 mismatch.

## Batteries

- **18650 Li-ion:** standard cells charge to 4.20 V (±50 mV) (BU-409), only between 0 and 45 °C, and never below 0 °C (BU-410). Discharge limits depend on the cell, typically −20 to 60 °C (BU-410): read your own cell's datasheet. Ready boards charge one cell.
- **LiFePO4:** 3.2 V cells charged to 3.65 V, 0 to 45 °C, discharged −20 to 60 °C, behind a protection circuit or BMS that stops charging at 3.7 V and discharging at 2 V (PSL LiFePO4). Li-ion chargers, including the one on every ready board here, charge to 4.20 V (BU-409, RAK19007), so a LiFePO4 cell must never sit on a board's battery socket while USB or solar can charge it: give it its own LiFePO4 charger and BMS, and power the node from that.
- RAK's base board datasheet lists no charging temperature limit and no battery temperature sensing (RAK19007), so assume it will charge a frozen cell. See [Battery chemistries](#ref/reference_battery_chemistry) and the town guide for cold.
- A Heltec V3 relay averaged 0.046 W (12 mA at 3.7 V) and ran six days on one 6.6 Wh cell (Kaspars solar).

## Box

Use plastic, not metal: Ebyte warns a metal case greatly cuts range, and wants the antenna exposed and vertical (Ebyte E22). Keep people at least 30 cm (1 ft) from the antenna of a node that is transmitting, and further from a 1 W module on a gain antenna: the US general-public limit at 915 MHz is 0.61 mW/cm² (f/1500, 47 CFR 1.1310), and 1 W into a 0 dBi antenna already gives 0.2 mW/cm² at 20 cm. Sealed boxes can suck in water as they heat and cool; a membrane vent equalises pressure without letting moisture in (Hylec vents).
